SRBMiner 3.8.5 refuses the card, with the reason spelled out once a pty is attached: "Found 1 OpenCL platforms, but none is AMD, NVIDIA OR INTEL". rusticl reports its platform vendor as Mesa, and SRBMiner filters on that string. Also learned: SRBMiner writes nothing to a pipe at all - exit 0 with zero lines - so every miner probe needs script -qec or it looks like a silent crash. Testing lolMiner, onezerominer and xmrig OpenCL for one that accepts a Mesa-vendor platform.

Miner verdict on Mint: lolMiner reports "OpenCL driver detected. Number of OpenCL supported GPUs: 0"; onezerominer says "No Supported GPU found"; SRBMiner says "Found 1 OpenCL platforms, but none is AMD, NVIDIA OR INTEL". Setting RUSTICL_ENABLE=radeonsi changes none of it - the refusal is a platform-VENDOR string filter (Mesa), not a missing device. xmrig is not a candidate at all: its OpenCL backend never covered RandomX.

What others actually do, from their own trackers: (1) hydrahive 0.6.2 (closed 2026-10-04) hit the identical wall on an RX 470 - srbminer "OpenCL not found", lolminer "Number of OpenCL supported GPUs: 0" - and their fix was to set RUSTICL_ENABLE=radeonsi for AMD miners plus report missing OpenCL honestly; they explicitly did NOT verify mining on real hardware through rusticl. (2) firominer PR #25 fixes the same class of bug by identifying GPUs through PCI vendor IDs instead of platform names - possible only in an open-source miner. (3) lolMiner changelog treats Polaris (RX 400/500) Linux mining as PAL/proprietary-driver territory and recommends modern drivers reporting HSA1.1 LC.

Practice check on Polaris + Linux: it is not Mesa at all. Mining OS images (HiveOS and friends) ship AMD proprietary amdgpu-pro OpenCL for gfx803. On stock Mint 22.3 that means scavenging legacy amdgpu-pro packages and grafting them in, with real ABI risk - versus Windows, where the RX 590 runs AMD own driver, OpenCL reports vendor AMD, and SRBMiner/lolMiner/unMiner all accept it as shipped. GPU mining is the workload where the OS choice is decided by the driver vendor rather than by preference. (Filed as event: "finding" is not a trail kind.)

Proved the RX 590 computes on Mint, so the card is not the problem: a C probe on rusticl built an OpenCL C kernel from SOURCE, ran it, and returned out[0]=1.0 out[1023]=1024.0. Device vendor reports AMD, id 0x1002, type GPU, OpenCL 3.0 / C 1.2. What rusticl refuses is a precompiled native binary via clCreateProgramWithBinary, and what the miners refuse is the platform vendor string "Mesa/X.org". lolMiner, SRBMiner and onezerominer ship precompiled gfx803 kernels, so on Mesa 25 (clover removed, rusticl only) there is no overlap between what they send and what the driver accepts.

Tried the string hack and it failed honestly: patched a private copy of libRusticlOpenCL.so.1.0.0 (Mesa/X.org -> AMD, same length, loaded via OCL_ICD_VENDORS). Result CL_UNKNOWN_ERROR getting the platform count - rusticl does not survive that edit, so the ICD was removed and the system left untouched. No binary-level shortcut exists.

The Windows OpenCL blocker was not a missing driver: Windows Update had installed only the display half, but the AMD payload was sitting in DriverStore (u0390451.inf_amd64_..B390182) with amdocl64.dll and 97 dlls in it. Copying that payload to C:AIopencl, registering HKLMSOFTWAREKhronosOpenCLVendors and adding the folder to PATH produced a working platform: "AMD Accelerated Parallel Processing / Advanced Micro Devices, Inc." - the exact string SRBMiner and lolMiner look for. So a machine can have full AMD OpenCL without ever running an AMD installer.

With OpenCL up, SRBMiner on Windows enumerates the card properly: GPU0 radeon_rx_590_series [ellesmere] [8192 MB] [CU: 36] [MaxBuf: 6745 MB]. It then refused pearl with "Algorithm pearlhash not supported on GPU0" - pearl is a newer-GPU kernel, not a driver problem. So the Mint failure and the Windows failure were different failures: on Mint the miner never saw the card, on Windows it sees the card and simply lacks that algorithm.

AMD still ships a Polaris/Vega branch in 2026: whql-amd-software-adrenalin-edition-26.5.2-win11-may-vega-polaris.exe, linked from the RX 590 support page. drivers.amd.com answers a bare curl with a 302 to Download-Incomplete; the same URL with a browser User-Agent and a Referer header returns 206 and the file. Anyone who concludes "the legacy driver is gone" from a plain curl is wrong.

The Windows box went off the network twice for two different reasons. First: sleep - robert is a desktop with S3 available and the balanced plan was still armed, so it slept mid-session. Fixed at firmware-request level (standby/monitor/disk timeouts 0x0, hibernation off via powercfg /h off, HiberbootEnabled=0, CsEnabled=0, high performance plan). Second: Windows Defender quarantined SRBMiner-MULTI.exe at 18:17 as Trojan:Win32/Bearfoos.D!ml - an ML false positive - so the next run reported "cannot find the file" and looked like a path bug. C:AIminers is now excluded and the exe restored from the zip.

Mining economics, measured against live data rather than guessed: ETC network 224.4 TH/s, 12.46 s blocks, 2.048 ETC reward, $6.90 - so the network emits ~$98k/day and one MH/s is worth $0.000437/day. An RX 590 at 24-32 MH/s earns $0.011-0.014/day. At ~276 W at the wall that is 6.64 kWh/day, which costs $0.66-$1.00/day at $0.10-$0.15/kWh. Net about -$29/month. Break-even needs 2,280 MH/s (81 cards) or power at $0.0018/kWh. Recommendation filed: robert idles as the LLM and media node at ~70 W; mining stays on 123 where the 6800 lives.

One-socket budget: 15 A at 120 V is 1800 W, safe continuous 1440 W. robert mining 276 W, 123 with the 6800 mining ~380 W, .134 idle ~100 W, .149 ~120 W, a 6-drive Proxmox NAS ~180 W = ~1050 W, which fits with nothing else on that circuit.

robert answered the mining question that Mint refused: with OpenCL alive, SRBMiner enumerates radeon_rx_590_series [ellesmere] [8192 MB] [CU: 36]. Standalone pearl was refused (no gfx803 kernel), but unMiner chose algorithm quantus and is hashing GPU-only at 90.4 MH/s (hashrate.cpu 0, total_gpu_workers 1) against quantus.unmineable.com:3333 with worker unmineable_miner_gmilnna. Duplicate OpenCL platforms, not duplicate hardware: with my hand-registered C:AIopencl ICD the card listed as GPU0 [0][0] and GPU1 [1][0] both at 01:00.0, and etchash built two 4.4 GB DAGs in 8 GB of VRAM - 2.72 MH/s at 89 W. Deleting the registry value left one device and 7.56 MH/s. Windows and PnP both report exactly one display adapter the whole time. Lesson filed in gpu-mining-setup.

tiny11 has no Visual C++ runtime, and that is why nothing ran: msvcp140/vcruntime140/vcruntime140_1/concrt140 all absent, llama-cli.exe --version exit -1073741515 (0xC0000135 STATUS_DLL_NOT_FOUND) with zero output, sd-cli --help the same. Measured after: llama.cpp b12192 sees Vulkan0 Radeon RX 590 Series 8192 MiB and generates at 33.2 t/s (prompt 38.3 t/s) on Bonsai-1.7B; sd-cli reports 307 help lines with vid_gen, --audio-vae, --llm and Wan2.2 TI2V 5B temporal_decode_frames.

Wan2.2 TI2V-5B (3.27 GB DiT + 1.34 GB VAE + 3.49 GB umt5) is the only one of the three that fits this box; LTX-2.3/2.5 costs more because its Gemma-3/4-12B text encoder is roughly 7 GB on its own.

nodes.title: Phoenix Cycle: a registration registry like Event_Handler and the Process Manager
nodes.intent: Phoenix is not a scheduler that knows what maintenance is - it is a registry that runs entries raised by their owners, exactly as Event_Handler and the Process Manager work. Every entry carries BOTH surfaces: an in-process tick thread the owner implements and an HTTP port the owner answers, because a thread-only entry is an invisible background process (forbidden) and a port-only entry needs a caller to remember it (the thing this module exists to remove). Triggers are declared - every / cron / on(event) / after(DAG refs) - never inferred. Every run leaves a receipt, every action runs under a lease so one slow entry cannot starve the rest, and the whole cycle plus its children stops on one close button. An empty registry is correct on a fresh install. Spec written at docs/spec/phoenix-registry.md. Done means: registry.json is honoured, six seed code entries plus two nag entries run and leave receipts, a nag surfaces one at a time in the monitor with TL;DR buttons, and stopping the cycle cancels outstanding leases honestly.

DECISION (operator, 2026-11-07): not a front end bolted onto stock Mint - a custom Mint-based ISO whose ONLY visible interface is the arcade front end. Operator words: "a custom mint backend mame machine front end iso installer - perfect!". So the deliverable is a bootable installer image: install it, reboot, and the machine is an arcade cabinet.

Build shape for that ISO: Mint base remastered with Cubic (boot the ISO in a VM, chroot, inject packages and scripts, rebuild squashfs) rather than live-build, because Mint tooling and package versions should stay as Mint ships them. Into the chroot go: mame pinned to the ROM set, xorg plus a bare compositor, the kiosk frontend, plymouth splash, an autologin user, and a systemd user unit that starts the frontend as the only session. No desktop environment on the target, even if Mint ships one - the desktop is the thing being hidden.

Frontend contract: a full-screen SDL/pygame selector listing ROMs with MAME snapshot art, driven by keyboard or USB gamepad, Enter launches. It reads a last_game file; on boot it shows "continue: <title>" for a few seconds and then execs MAME, and only an explicit key press drops into the grid. That wrapper is the whole difference between a laptop with an emulator and a cabinet - no stock front end (Attract Mode, EmulationStation, Pegasus) boots back into the last game.

Provisioning/open questions to settle before building the ISO: where ROMs live (baked in only if the set is small; otherwise one SD card or USB per machine, with a first-boot scan), which MAME version the operator ROM set matches (mismatch boots black screens), per-machine input config (USB gamepad ctrlr file, since laptop keyboards ghost past ~3 keys), and the boot-time target (BIOS to gameplay under 25 s on the slowest laptop that still holds full frame rate).

Transfer notes for a Wi-Fi node in another room: hydra seed (module/ minus every module/*/data so the node cannot inherit the controller identity, logs or DAG) 148.7 MB and electron dist 158.5 MB both moved in ~20 s each; HF model pulls ran at ~10 MB/s until the CDN started holding 0-byte files, which is why the MOSS encoder is now fetched with -C - in a retry loop plus --speed-limit/--speed-time so a dead connection aborts instead of hanging.

BUG (found 2026-11-07 on robert, fixed same night): the standby guard steals the GPU from an active render. Root cause is a two-part miss in scripts/standby-guard.ps1. (1) Its AI-process list was @(audiocpp_cli, audiocpp_server, audiocpp_gguf, llama-server, llama-cli, sd-server, sd) - sd-cli was absent, and sd-cli is what every still and video render on these nodes actually runs. The guard therefore saw NO AI work while a 5B video model was sampling, and (2) its ResumeGraceSeconds default was 45 s. Result: 45 seconds into a render it launched unMiner, the card went from 46 s/it to 158 s/it, and Windows reset the driver with "ggml_vulkan: device lost on Vulkan0 / vk::Queue::submit: ErrorDeviceLost" thirteen steps in.

BUG FIX: (a) sd-cli, llama-bench and whisper-cli added to the guard AI-process list, so a batch render is recognised as work the moment it appears; (b) default grace raised from 45 s to 1800 s - the operator rule is 30 minutes of no activity before the miner may resume ("wait 30 min for no activity before restarting miner... for this exact reason"); (c) the guard now reads this node standby.after from module/Menu/data/node.json when -ResumeGraceSeconds is not passed explicitly, so the declared number in a node identity actually drives the behaviour instead of a script constant. Both nodes set to 1800.

BUG EVIDENCE: Hydra ProcessWrapper rows standby-guard-016-5598, standby-miner-022-a041 and standby-miner-017-25d9 were the launchers (pids 12128, 13108, 13828) - not a scheduled task, not a Run key, not the Startup folder, which were all checked and empty. Killing the guard and miner rows through the ProcessWrapper API and then re-running the render is the reproduction test: steps return to ~46 s/it with the guard gone.

Related environment fault found in the same incident: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\GraphicsDrivers\TdrDelay was unset, i.e. the 2-second Windows default, so any submit that slows past 2 s under contention triggers a driver reset and sd.cpp reports "device lost" with no OOM and no model error. Set to 60 s on robert (takes effect at reboot). Worth checking on every Windows GPU node before blaming the model for a mid-run death.

ROBERT BOOTS ITSELF, end to end, proved by an actual reboot. Chain measured: (1) Winlogon AutoAdminLogon=1 + ForceAutoLogon=1 + DefaultUserName=User + DefaultDomainName=DESKTOP-AAJBDVJ + DefaultPassword set -> quser reports "user console 1 Active" and one explorer process, so no password was ever typed and no lock screen appeared; (2) the Hydra V2 shortcut in the Startup folder raised relaunch-hydra.cmd -> 14 node + 6 electron processes, 7/7 doors listening; (3) the standby guard assumed idle at boot and started unMiner THROUGH ProcessWrapper -> standby-miner row, then adopted the three unMiner children and SRBMiner as rows; (4) quantus at 91.2 MH/s 1-min, 90.6 MH/s on gpu0, cpu workers 0, first share accepted in 100 s.

The fleet password is a design, not a secret: user User with password "unknown", local Administrator, never expires. It was verified without logging anyone in - LogonUser(LOGON32_LOGON_NETWORK) for DESKTOP-AAJBDVJ\User returned a token (VALID) while empty string, "password" and "user" were rejected with win32 1326. That is why the auto-logon can be trusted rather than hoped for: the registry value is the account real credential.

BUG, and a nasty one because it looked like "mining will not start": a trailing comma after the AiProcs array in the standby-guard param block made the script un-parseable, so EVERY guard launch died instantly. ProcessWrapper saw a dead row, raised another, and left seven stacked standby-guard rows (016-022) with no log lines at all - the guard never reached its first LogIt. The fix is one character, and the rule is now: parse a PowerShell file with [System.Management.Automation.Language.Parser]::ParseFile before shipping it, because a .ps1 that cannot parse fails with no process, no log and no error anywhere the operator would look.

BUG: two guards can be raised for one node (the app watchdog table plus any row started by hand) and they fight over the miner - one stopping it while the other starts it. Fixed with a named mutex Global\hydra-standby-guard taken for the life of the process; a second guard exits immediately. Verified by deliberately raising two: the second was gone within 12 s and the first carried on mining.

WAN2.2 HERO RENDER SUCCEEDED on the RX 590: 704x416 x 33 frames, 24 steps, cfg 5.0, flow-shift 3.0, --vae-tiling --temporal-tiling, seed 7 -> generate_video completed in 999.59 s, C:\AI\ads\wan22-hero3.webm, 973 KB VP8, EXITCODE 0. Frames 4/16/28 are a coherent photorealistic workbench shot: a graphics card on a pale wooden surface, warm lamp light from the left, cables blurred in the background, shallow depth of field. First-to-last-frame PSNR 32.15 dB, so there is real (gentle) motion rather than a freeze. The three earlier attempts and their distinct causes: miner contention + 2 s TdrDelay (device lost at step 13), VAE weight staging without tiling (decode failed), device lost again at step 18 until TdrDelay=60 was armed by a reboot.

MOSS-IMAGE WORKS ON THE 590 - the known-good recipe from the earlier Mint work carried over unchanged. 1024x1024, cfg-scale 3.0, seed 11, four files (DiT Q4_K + Qwen3.5-9B Q4_K_M encoder + flux2-vae + external tokenizer), --offload-to-cpu: generate_image completed in 1215.34 s, VAE decode 15.27 s, 20 steps at 59.25 s/it, C:\AI\ads\moss-hero.png 1.87 MB EXITCODE 0. The picture is a coherent photorealistic upright cabinet in a dim garage: overhead bulb, concrete floor, shelves and boxes lost in background blur, film grain and vignette. Honest gaps: the marquee is a glowing smear rather than legible art and the CRT shows light instead of a game - expected for "no text" in the negative, and the next pass should either ask for an empty screen explicitly or paint the art in afterwards.

Cost of that still, for planning: 20 minutes of RX 590 wall time per 1024x1024 image at 20 steps. That is the fp32 tax on Polaris - no fp16, no int dot, no matrix cores - so MOSS on this box is a batch/turnaround tool, not an interactive one. If stills become a regular need on robert, lodestones/Kromoss (same four-file layout plus an 8-step DMD LoRA) is the shortcut worth trying next, and it drops into the same command.

THE YIELD WORKS END TO END, observed live rather than reasoned about: with the miner running from the boot chain, starting sd-cli produced "YIELD stopped standby-miner-028-06e9 through ProcessWrapper", "YIELD miner stopped for AI work", "mode -> ai [sd-cli(12168,gpu,working)]" within one 15 s poll. And a fresh guard started while the render was in flight logged "boot: work already on the card (sd-cli(12168,gpu,working)) - miner stays down" - the boot rule is conditional on the card really being free, not a blind start.

New node gap worth remembering: module/*/data is excluded from the seed so a node cannot inherit identity, but that also drops module/Event_Handler/data/palette.json, and an empty palette answers every POST /api/events/trigger with 404 - the guard silently lost its standby.yield and standby.resume records for a whole render. Copying the palette is not enough on its own: the Event door reads it once at start, so the app has to be restarted (or the door) before the names exist. Robert now reports 7 events: job.done, job.submitted, shelf.pulled, shelf.refused, standby.pin, standby.resume, standby.yield.
